title: Local history booklet; personal and family data
description: Alba Libera Marra shows the interviewer a fourth-grade social studies booklet she compiled of pioneer stories about the Kellogg area, mentioning Sister Rose Frances and the Catawba mission school. The interviewer then fills out a personal data sheet, recording Alba's 1912 birth at Silver King (Government Gulch) and details about her Italian-born mother and her father, Dominic Marra, who worked as a miner, smelter man and custodian. She also notes her mother lost several stillborn babies in the mining camp.

title: Education; teaching and administrative career
description: Alba traces her schooling from Lewiston Normal through the University of Washington, Central Washington, and master's work at the University of Idaho. She describes becoming a teaching principal at Sunnyside in 1941, supervising student teachers at the University of Utah, and returning to Kellogg as elementary coordinator. After the 1952 consolidation she supervised thirteen elementary buildings and continued teaching summer courses in Montana, totaling 44 years in education.

title: Hobbies; organizations; small-town life
description: Alba lists her pastimes of sewing, reading, visiting nursing homes, and her memberships in business and professional women's groups, Delta Kappa Gamma and the PTA, which gave her a life membership in 1963. She shares an anecdote about fabric that smelled of natural gas. She then reflects on the benefits of rural community life, arguing that small towns offer better security and recognition than big cities.

title: Family moves; farm life at Prosser
description: Alba recounts her family's moves to Sacramento and then to a farm at Prosser, Washington, where her father broke his leg and her mother ran the orchard and milked cows. She describes rattlesnakes by the canal, fear of tramps who hopped trains and begged for food, and the primitive outhouse her mother had to empty. The farm failed when the apples froze, and the family returned by boxcar to their unsold Kellogg home.

title: Father's health; Depression-era thrift
description: Alba explains that her father left mining for smelter work because of lead poisoning and lung damage, and that he later kept a beloved greenhouse. She describes the family's financial straits after losing the farm, her mother washing and ironing for miners' boarding houses by candlelight, and her own part-time secretarial work at thirty-five cents an hour while in school.

title: Childhood recreation; trips to town
description: Alba recalls her father telling fairy tales, families gathering for picnics, and children inventing their own games, including pretending a writing desk was a piano and hypnotizing each other. She describes walking the three miles from Silver King to Kellogg every Saturday for shopping and the matinee, riding stages and trains, and attending traveling Chautauqua shows and plays at the Liberty Theater.

title: Harsh winters; first circus; faster childhoods; women's farm work
description: Alba recalls hand-shoveling huge snow drifts and traveling by car to Wallace for her first circus. She notes that modern children grow up faster with television and internet, then describes how Prosser women combined home and farm work with cooperative help for neighbors.

title: Neighborhood picnics; community decline; hard times and insurance gaps
description: She remembers Sunday horse-and-buggy picnics shared among Italian and other farm families, always timed around feeding animals, and laments that those neighborhoods have emptied. She then explains how families before Social Security and health insurance had to save desperately against illness or a breadwinner's death.

title: Widows and boarding houses; staying single; wartime regret
description: Widows including a friend whose husband died in a mine disaster took in boarders to survive. Alba explains she never felt pressured to marry, idolized independent teachers, and valued her freedom, though married people had easier social lives; she also regrets staying to teach instead of joining the wartime service.

title: College life at Lewiston; transportation changes; frugality and credit
description: She describes strict dorm life at Lewiston, locked in nightly and signing in and out, traveling home only at Christmas by train, and contrasts that era's better public transit with today's poor service. Depression experiences made her frugal, though she now uses credit cards carefully, and she recalls her parents paying for a home, car, and her mother's surgery in cash.

title: Childhood chores; family size; early retirement
description: She remembers household chores and the playhouse her father built from dynamite boxes, and approves of women's modern ability to limit family size. After her friend developed cancer, she retired two years early while healthy, reflecting on being an unmarried only child.

title: Europe trip plans; Italian relatives; language worries
description: Alba outlines her first trip to Europe, visiting a 79-year-old cousin in Italy before a TWA getaway tour from London that a retired teacher friend will join. She worries about three weeks speaking only Italian, describes corresponding with relatives, and frames retirement as a graduation into something new.
